title: Special Tests, Diagnostic Accuracy and Imaging
lead: What a "positive test" really means, and when imaging helps.

sections.title: 4.1 Why no single test is perfect

blocks.text: Every special test sometimes misses a condition that is present (a false negative) and sometimes flags a condition that is not present (a false positive). Understanding how often this happens tells you how much to trust a result.

sections.title: 4.2 The four key words, with a simple example

blocks.text: Imagine 100 patients with knee pain. 20 truly have a meniscal tear. A test is performed on all 100.
This example uses invented teaching numbers only.

items: **Sensitivity** = true positives ÷ all who have the condition = 15/20 = 75%. How good the test is at catching the condition.
**Specificity** = true negatives ÷ all who do not have it = 64/80 = 80%. How good the test is at clearing people who are healthy.
**SnNout**: a highly **S**ensitive test, when **N**egative, helps rule **out**.
**SpPin**: a highly **S**pecific test, when **P**ositive, helps rule **in**.

blocks.label: MEMORY HOOK
body: "SnNout and SpPin". Sensitive tests are good screens; specific tests are good confirmers.

sections.title: 4.3 Likelihood ratios: the most useful number

blocks.text: A likelihood ratio (LR) tells you how much a test result changes the probability of a condition.
These ranges are widely taught thresholds [Ref – to verify]. In this book, accuracy values for individual tests are marked [Ref – to verify] until checked against current systematic reviews.

sections.title: 4.4 Pre-test probability: why context changes the meaning of a test

blocks.text: A positive test in a patient whose history strongly suggests the condition is far more convincing than the same positive test in a patient with an unlikely history. Your history sets the pre-test probability; the test only moves it up or down.

blocks.label: TEACHER'S VOICE
body: Never let one test overturn a strong clinical picture. If the history shouts "rotator cuff tear" and one test is negative, your probability falls a little, not to zero. Ask: does the rest of the picture still fit?

sections.title: 4.5 Test clusters and clinical prediction rules

blocks.text: Combining tests usually improves accuracy. A cluster such as "three of four tests positive" can be more specific than any single test. Clinical prediction rules (for example the Ottawa ankle rules or the Canadian C-spine rule) combine history and examination findings to guide a decision such as whether to X-ray. Use the version and thresholds exactly as the original source defined them.

sections.title: 4.6 Symptom reproduction versus a diagnostic positive

blocks.text: A test that reproduces pain tells you that the tissues loaded are sensitive. It does not identify which structure is damaged. For example, many shoulder "impingement" tests load several tissues at once. Interpret every test as "supports" or "makes less likely", never as "proves".

blocks.label: COMMON STUDENT TRAP
body: Disc bulges, degeneration and rotator cuff changes are common in people without pain, and become more common with age [Ref – to verify]. An MRI "finding" is not automatically the cause of the patient's pain. Match imaging to the clinical picture.

items: Suspected fracture meeting a validated decision rule.
Red flags suggesting tumour, infection, cauda equina or cord compression.
Failure of an adequate trial of conservative care when imaging would change management (for example surgical consideration).

blocks.text: Routine imaging for non-specific low back pain without red flags is not recommended by major guidelines [Ref – to verify].

items: **A test has high sensitivity. It is negative. What can you conclude?** The condition becomes less likely (SnNout), especially if the pre-test probability was low.
**A test has high specificity and is positive. What can you conclude?** The condition becomes more likely (SpPin).
**An MRI shows a disc bulge at L4 to L5 in a patient with central back pain only. Is the bulge the cause?** Not necessarily. Bulges are common in pain-free people. The clinical findings decide.
**Why are clusters useful?** Combining tests improves the ability to rule in or out compared with single tests.
**When should you avoid repeating a provocative test?** When it has already clearly reproduced the symptoms, or when irritability is high.

sections.title: Now You Should Be Able To

items: Explain sensitivity, specificity, SnNout, SpPin and likelihood ratios in your own words.
Explain why pre-test probability changes test meaning.
Decide when imaging is appropriate and explain incidental findings to patients.
